title: Pharmacist Prescribing of Hormonal Contraceptive Patches and Self-Administered Oral Hormonal Contraceptives, and Dispensing Expedited Partner Therapy for Chlamydia
topic: Pharmacist prescribing and expedited partner therapy / Contraceptive prescribing under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F and chlamydia partner prescriptions
subtopic: The authority in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(a) as rewritten in 2025 and what s. 19F(b) and (c) direct the Department's rules to establish, require and prohibit; the conditions adopted in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15); the requirements for hormonal contraceptive patches and oral hormonal contraceptives in Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125; the practitioner authority for expedited partner therapy in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B and 105 CMR 700.003(H); the partner prescription under 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) and 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7), 721.070(C) and 721.020(D)(4); the dispensing procedures of Policy 2020-08; and, briefly, the stocking and filling of family planning prescriptions under Board Policy 2023-05 and 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) and the MassHealth over-the-counter contraceptive standing order under M.G.L. c. 118E, s. 83
learning_objectives: State who may prescribe and dispense under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(a)(i), which contraceptive products the authority reaches, and why a previous practitioner prescription is not a precondition.
Separate what s. 19F(b) and (c) direct the Department's rules to contain from what 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) makes operative, and apply the distinction to the clinical-visit time frame.
List the five requirements of 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b) and the appointment prohibition in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(c), and place each in time relative to prescribing and dispensing.

Apply the conditions in Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 that the statute and regulation do not state: FDA-approved products whether over-the-counter or prescription-only, patients of any age, the 12-month supply ceiling, refills without a clinical visit, the NPI, documentation and the single-location condition on the registration statement.
Describe the training a pharmacist completes before prescribing: Board approval, the five objectives, the recommended accreditation and the documentation to be provided upon request.
Identify who may provide expedited partner therapy under 105 CMR 700.003(H) and for which infection, and explain how the authorization in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B differs in reach.

State what a separate partner prescription bears where the patient's name and address would be noted, and read 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) and Policy 2020-08 together with the electronic prescribing exception, the pharmacist's position on verifying it, and the blank name-and-address allowance in 105 CMR 721.000.

Apply Policy 2020-08, as dispensing procedures under the authority in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B and 105 CMR 700.003(H), to the pharmacy profile and label for an expedited partner therapy prescription, and state what a pharmacist who is unable or unwilling to fill one must do.

Distinguish pharmacist prescribing under s. 19F from dispensing under the MassHealth standing order authorized by M.G.L. c. 118E, s. 83, and state what Board Policy 2023-05 expects when a valid prescription for a family planning medication cannot be filled at once.
Recognise where the official texts are silent, such as a blood pressure reading or the contents of the written record, and choose the course that is safe on any reading.

orientation.text: This section covers two things a Massachusetts pharmacist does outside the ordinary pattern of filling a practitioner's prescription for a named patient, and each rests on a different stack of law. The first is prescribing. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F lets a registered pharmacist prescribe and dispense hormonal contraceptive patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives; the Department of Public Health implemented it in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15), which grants the authority in accordance with guidance issued by the department; and the Department's current guidance on the subject is Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 of August 25, 2026. The second is dispensing expedited partner therapy, in which a practitioner treats the sex partner of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia without examining the partner. There the pharmacist is not the prescriber: M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B and 105 CMR 700.003(H) are the authority for the practitioner, the prescription format regulation in 105 CMR 721.000 addresses the partner prescription, and Policy 2020-08 sets out the pharmacy's dispensing procedures under that authority. Neighbouring subjects are only named here: emergency contraception dispensed under the statewide standing order; pharmacist prescribing of HIV prevention and sexually transmitted infection medications under s. 19F(a)(ii) and the Department's 2026 guidance on it; the Schedule VI prescription and prescription format in general; the container label and the dispensing record, including the December 2025 advisory on prescription labeling for reproductive and gender-affirming medications; counseling; pharmacist administration of medications; and collaborative drug therapy management.

Section 19F was inserted in chapter 94C by section 42 of chapter 28 of the Acts of 2023, and that act took effect as of July 1, 2023 except where it specified otherwise, which it did not for section 42. Subsection (a) was struck out and replaced by section 39 of chapter 14 of the Acts of 2025, an emergency law approved on August 5, 2025, and its clause (i) now provides that, notwithstanding any general or special law to the contrary, a registered pharmacist may prescribe and dispense hormonal contraceptive patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives to any person, regardless of whether the person has evidence of a previous prescription from a primary care practitioner or reproductive health care practitioner for such a product. Three features of clause (i) decide most questions. The authority belongs to the registered pharmacist. It reaches two kinds of product, patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives, and the Department's letter confirms that only FDA-approved medications authorized by s. 19F and contained in the letter may be prescribed by a pharmacist. And the words regardless of whether the person has evidence of a previous prescription mean the pharmacist is not limited to continuing therapy another practitioner started. Clause (ii), added in 2025, concerns medications for HIV and sexually transmitted infections, and it is a separate subject not taught here. A different route rests on M.G.L. c. 118E, s. 83 rather than s. 19F: a licensed pharmacist may dispense an over-the-counter oral contraceptive to a MassHealth member or Health Safety Net patient in accordance with a standing order issued by a practitioner registered under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 7 and designated by the assistant secretary for the division, and shall submit a claim to MassHealth or the HSN. The MassHealth standing order signed and dated January 27, 2025 covers norgestrel 0.075 mg tablets, up to a 365-day supply, for a member or patient who states that they are of reproductive potential and age, under a protocol pharmacists must follow and with records of dispensing maintained in the patient profile of the pharmacy dispensing system.

Subsections (b) and (c) of s. 19F are addressed to rulemaking rather than directly to the pharmacist. Under s. 19F(b) the department, in consultation with the board of registration in medicine, the board of registration in pharmacy and the division of medical assistance, and in consideration of guidelines established by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, shall adopt rules to establish standard procedures for pharmacist prescribing of these products and the time frame in which a patient shall have evidence, as defined by the department, of a clinical visit from a primary care practitioner or reproductive health care practitioner immediately following a previous prescription and dispensation of such a product by a pharmacist. Section 19F(c) then says what those rules shall do. They shall require a pharmacist to complete a training program approved by the board of registration in pharmacy that is related to prescribing these products; to provide a self-screening risk assessment tool that the patient shall use before the pharmacist prescribes; to refer the patient to the patient's primary care practitioner or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable, upon prescribing and dispensing, or advise the patient to consult with such a practitioner; to provide the patient with a written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; and to dispense the product as soon as practicable after the pharmacist issues the prescription. They shall prohibit a pharmacist from requiring a patient to schedule an appointment with the pharmacist for the prescribing or dispensing, and from prescribing and dispensing to a patient who previously received a prescription and dispensation of such a product by a pharmacist and who does not have evidence of a clinical visit within the time frame established under s. 19F(b)(ii). Each of these is a statement of what the rules shall contain, so whether a requirement binds a pharmacist depends on what the Department adopted.

Within 105 CMR 700.000, which the Department's letter identifies as implementing s. 19F, the provision is 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15), and it sits in 105 CMR 700.004(B) under the heading Exemptions from Requirement to Register. Paragraph (15) provides that a registered pharmacist may prescribe and dispense hormonal contraceptive patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives to any person, in accordance with guidance issued by the department. Subparagraph (a) allows this regardless of whether the person has evidence of a previous prescription, provided all requirements of subparagraphs (b) and (c) are met. Subparagraph (b) requires a registered pharmacist prescribing these products to complete a training program approved by the board of registration in pharmacy prior to prescribing; to provide a self-screening risk assessment tool that the patient shall use prior to the pharmacist prescribing; to refer the patient to the patient's primary care practitioner or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable, upon prescribing and dispensing, or advise the patient to consult with one; to provide the patient with a written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; and to dispense it as soon as practicable after the pharmacist issues the prescription. Subparagraph (c) provides that a pharmacist shall not require a patient to schedule an appointment with the pharmacist for the prescribing or dispensing. What paragraph (15) leaves out matters as much. It states no clinical-visit time frame, does not say what counts as evidence of a clinical visit, and contains no prohibition on prescribing for a returning patient who lacks such evidence, so the statute's direction on that point has not been carried into the published regulation.

Because paragraph (15) grants the authority in accordance with guidance issued by the department, the conditions in the Department's guidance are part of the terms on which the regulation grants it, although the guidance is not itself a regulation. The current letter, Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125, is dated August 25, 2026, comes from the Director of the Bureau of Health Professions Licensure, and rescinds and replaces DCP 25-04-124. It covers pharmacist prescribing of contraceptives, HIV prevention medications and sexually transmitted infection medications, and it opens with two statements that frame the rest: there is no requirement to prescribe these medications, and a pharmacist is not required to obtain a Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration as long as the prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location. Its General Prescribing Requirements, which precede the product sections, state that only FDA-approved medications authorized by s. 19F and contained in the letter may be prescribed by a pharmacist; that the pharmacist must obtain a National Provider Identifier; that patient counseling and education are conducted on the proper use, risks and side effects of the selected product; that the medication is prescribed only in accordance with the manufacturer's approved labeling or statewide guidance; that the patient is provided a written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; that the product is dispensed as soon as practicable after the pharmacist issues the prescription; that all activities related to the prescribing and dispensing are documented and readily available; that the patient is referred to, or advised to consult with, a clinical provider, or, if the patient consents, the pharmacist notifies the patient's primary care practitioner; and that the pharmacist must maintain continued competency regarding current guidelines. Pharmacists are encouraged to enroll in MassHealth for the limited purpose of ordering and referring so that their prescriptions can be reimbursed for MassHealth enrollees. Counseling duties in general are taught separately.

Under its heading for hormonal contraceptive patches and oral hormonal contraceptives, the letter states that a pharmacist may prescribe these products, regardless of whether the product is over-the-counter or prescription-only, to patients of any age, and it attaches five items to that statement. Before prescribing, the patient completes a pharmacy-provided self-screening risk assessment tool based on the current United States Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use. A valid prescription is generated for up to, but not more than, a 12-month supply. Lack of a clinical visit with a primary care practitioner or reproductive health care practitioner does not preclude the pharmacist from issuing a prescription with refills. A scheduled appointment with the pharmacist shall not be required for the prescribing or dispensing. And before prescribing, the pharmacist completes a training program whose objectives must include describing the mechanism of action of hormonal contraceptive products and differentiating between their types, assessing patient eligibility for hormonal contraceptive use and recommended products, educating patients on proper use, risks and benefits of various contraceptive products, educating patients on strategies to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections, and documenting patient care visits related to these products. The letter recommends programs accredited by ACPE or IPCE rather than requiring accreditation, and it requires documentation of completed training to be provided upon request. The regulation adds that the program is to be one approved by the board of registration in pharmacy and completed prior to prescribing. A pharmacist therefore completes the training before the first prescription, confirms that the program addresses each of the five objectives, and keeps documentation that can be provided when asked.

Read together, the three layers settle the question the statute leaves most exposed. Section 19F(c)(ii)(B) directs the rules to prohibit prescribing for a patient who previously received a pharmacist prescription and lacks evidence of a clinical visit within a time frame the rules are to set; 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) sets no time frame and contains no such prohibition; and the Department's letter states that lack of a clinical visit does not preclude a pharmacist from issuing a prescription with refills. None of the three texts makes a clinical-visit bar operative, so a pharmacist who turns away a returning patient on that ground is applying a direction to rulemakers as if it were a rule, and any fixed period quoted for the bar has no source in them. The referral duty raises a different question, because there the guidance reads more loosely than the regulation. The regulation requires the pharmacist to refer the patient to a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable, or to advise the patient to consult one, while the letter also names notifying the patient's primary care practitioner, with consent, as an alternative. The course that satisfies both texts is to refer or advise in every case and to notify the primary care practitioner as well where the patient consents.

Several practical questions are not answered by the statute, the regulation or the letter, and the safe course follows from what they do say. None of them requires the pharmacist to take a blood pressure reading; the screening they require before prescribing is the patient's use of the pharmacy-provided self-screening tool, and the letter requires prescribing only in accordance with the manufacturer's approved labeling or statewide guidance, so a concern that the tool or the labeling raises is resolved before a prescription is issued. None of them lists the contents of the written record beyond the product prescribed and dispensed, so the safe record identifies that product and is handed to the patient. The authority is conferred on a registered pharmacist, and neither the statute nor the regulation extends it to a pharmacy intern or a pharmacy technician. The letter's 12-month ceiling does not say how refills count toward it, and keeping the whole supply a prescription authorizes, refills included, within 12 months complies on either reading. And the letter's registration statement is conditioned on prescribing and dispensing at a single pharmacy location without saying what applies otherwise, so the safe course is to dispense at the location where the pharmacist prescribes, or to ask the Drug Control Program before arranging anything else.

Expedited partner therapy starts with a practitioner, not a pharmacist. M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B directs the department, in consultation with the board of registration in medicine, to promulgate regulations authorizing a physician, physician assistant, nurse practitioner or certified nurse midwife who is authorized under chapter 94C to prescribe and dispense prescription drugs, and who diagnoses infections due to Chlamydia trachomatis and other sexually transmitted infections suitable for expedited partner treatment based on national standards, including the Center for Disease Control's Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines, and as further defined in regulation by the department, to prescribe and dispense such drugs to a patient's sexual partners for presumptive treatment without examining them. The words reaching other sexually transmitted infections came in through the amendments made by sections 113 and 114 of chapter 140 of the Acts of 2024, effective July 1, 2024, and they reach those infections as further defined in regulation. The regulation, 105 CMR 700.003(H), provides that a registered physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or nurse midwife may provide expedited partner therapy for the treatment of chlamydia infection, meaning the prescribing or dispensing for immediate treatment of an appropriate therapeutic agent in Schedule VI for the sex partner or partners of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia infection. It requires the prescribing or dispensing to accord with 105 CMR 700.003(H), the medical, physician assistant and advanced practice nursing regulations, and the applicable guidelines of the Department, the three practitioner boards and the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention; it requires a therapeutic agent the practitioner provides directly to be given in a separate, properly labeled container for the sex partner; and it requires the practitioner to counsel the patient about expedited partner therapy and, whenever possible, to provide a Department information sheet, or a comparable one, for the partner. A pharmacist is not among the practitioners the regulation names.

When the practitioner gives the patient a prescription for the partner rather than the drug, 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) requires a separate prescription for the sex partner, which includes on the prescription form, where the name and address of the patient is to be noted, either the name of the sex partner or the words 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT.' Policy 2020-08, citing 105 CMR 700.003(H), describes that separate prescription as provided in one of two ways: issued for the named sex partner or partners of the infected patient, or issued using 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the patient's name and address. The prescription format regulation deals with these prescriptions separately. 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) lists prescriptions issued pursuant to 105 CMR 700.003(J) for expedited partner therapy for treatment of chlamydia, intended for dispensing to the patient's partner, among those not required to be issued as electronic prescriptions, so they may be written or oral, an oral one being subject to 105 CMR 721.070(B); in the current text of 105 CMR 700.000, expedited partner therapy is provided for in 105 CMR 700.003(H), and 105 CMR 700.003(J) concerns medical device manufacturers. Under 105 CMR 721.070(C), a pharmacist who receives an otherwise valid written or oral prescription is not required to verify that it properly falls under one of the exceptions from the requirement to electronically prescribe. And 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) allows the patient's name and address to be left blank on a prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7). Read together, the format regulation excuses the name and address, and the expedited partner therapy regulation and the Board's policy say what stands in that place. A prescription whose patient field is simply empty, carrying neither the partner's name nor a designation, is not in the form 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) and Policy 2020-08 describe, and the safe course is to obtain the name or the designation from the prescriber before filling it.

The authority for expedited partner therapy is in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B and 105 CMR 700.003(H), and Policy 2020-08 sets out the dispensing procedures a pharmacy follows under that authority. The policy, which bears the names of the Board of Registration in Pharmacy and the Drug Control Program and was adopted on July 31, 2020, describes expedited partner therapy as treating the sex partners of people diagnosed with chlamydia infection without examining or testing the partner, and it states that it applies only to the treatment of chlamydia infection. For filling, it directs the pharmacy to create a patient profile and prescription label using 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the patient's name and address, so a partner prescription bearing a designation is profiled and labeled under that designation and not under the index patient's name. The policy states that instruction for expedited partner therapy prescriptions generally, without separately addressing a prescription that names the partner, and a pharmacist unsure how to profile that form can put the question to the Board, as the policy invites. The policy then gives one instruction for a pharmacist who will not fill: if a pharmacist is unable or unwilling to fill an expedited partner therapy prescription, the pharmacist must refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy. Sending the person back to the prescriber is not that referral. The contraceptive letter, by contrast, states that there is no requirement to prescribe and does not attach a comparable step to a decision not to prescribe.

A different question arises when a patient presents a valid contraceptive prescription written by another prescriber. Under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) a pharmacy shall maintain on its premises the equipment, supplies and medications necessary to conduct the practice of pharmacy in accordance with the usual needs of the community and the scope of practice of the pharmacy, and Board Policy 2023-05, Access to Reproductive Health Medications, effective March 22, 2023, states that all family planning medications, including emergency contraception and contraceptive prescriptions, are considered necessary to meet the usual needs of each and every community across the Commonwealth. The policy therefore states that all pharmacies located in Massachusetts and licensed by the Board must maintain a continuous, sufficient supply of family planning medications, and that where one is not immediately available for dispensing pursuant to a valid prescription or order, the licensed pharmacy and/or licensed pharmacist is responsible for ensuring the patient's access in a timely manner, by refilling stock, contacting the prescriber for a reasonable alternative medication, transferring the prescription to another pharmacy where the medication is readily available for dispensing, or some other manner such as mail order or central fill. It states that a licensed pharmacy and/or pharmacist that refuses to stock, dispense or fill any valid prescription or order for family planning medications, or impedes access to them in any way, will be in violation of 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) and practice standards, and that the Board will investigate such violations fully. That is Board policy applying the regulation, and it differs from both the expedited partner therapy referral route and the letter's statement that there is no requirement to prescribe. The policy's list of family planning medications also names mifepristone and misoprostol, whose dispensing is not taught in this section.

worked_examples.scenario: A 17-year-old walks into a pharmacy without an appointment and asks a trained pharmacist to prescribe a hormonal contraceptive patch. She has never had a contraceptive prescription. A technician tells her that contraception patients are seen by appointment only, that she must be 18, and that she needs a prescription from her own doctor first. The pharmacist overrules the technician on all three points, has her complete the self-screening tool, prescribes a 15-month supply of a patch that is in stock, and asks her to come back next week to collect it.
steps: Appointment: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(c) provides that a pharmacist shall not require a patient to schedule an appointment for the prescribing or dispensing, and Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 repeats that a scheduled appointment shall not be required, so the technician's first statement is wrong.
Age: the letter states that a pharmacist may prescribe these products to patients of any age, and neither s. 19F nor the regulation states an age limit, so a 17-year-old is not excluded.

Previous prescription: s. 19F(a)(i) and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(a) allow prescribing regardless of whether the person has evidence of a previous prescription, provided the regulation's requirements are met.
Screening and product: the patient uses the pharmacy-provided self-screening tool before the pharmacist prescribes, and a patch is one of the two product types the authority reaches.
Supply: the letter provides for a valid prescription for up to, but not more than, a 12-month supply, so a 15-month supply exceeds it.

Timing: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b)5 requires the pharmacist to dispense as soon as practicable after issuing the prescription, and deferring an in-stock patch to next week does not meet that requirement.

After prescribing and dispensing, the pharmacist provides the written record and refers the patient to a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable, or advises her to consult one.
worked_examples.resolution: The pharmacist was right to reject the technician's three conditions but erred twice: the prescription may not exceed a 12-month supply, and a product on the shelf must be dispensed as soon as practicable. The error the scenario invites is to treat workflow preferences, an assumed age limit or a prior prescription as conditions the texts impose, while missing the two conditions they do impose.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient received a pharmacist-prescribed oral hormonal contraceptive 14 months ago and has not seen any practitioner since. The pharmacy's written procedure says that under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F a pharmacist may not prescribe again unless the patient shows evidence of a clinical visit within 12 months of the first pharmacist prescription, and the pharmacist on duty declines on that basis.
steps: Read s. 19F(c)(ii)(B) for what it is: it directs the rules adopted under s. 19F(b) to prohibit prescribing to such a patient, measured by a time frame those rules are to establish under s. 19F(b)(ii).
Look at what the Department adopted: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) sets no clinical-visit time frame, does not define evidence of a clinical visit, and contains no such prohibition.

Look at the Department's guidance: Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 states that lack of a clinical visit with a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner does not preclude a pharmacist from issuing a prescription with refills.
Test the procedure's 12 months against the texts: neither the statute, the regulation nor the letter states that period.

Apply the conditions that do operate: the self-screening tool before prescribing, prescribing in accordance with the labeling or statewide guidance, the 12-month supply ceiling, the written record, dispensing as soon as practicable, and referral or advice to consult a practitioner.
worked_examples.resolution: No operative clinical-visit rule bars a new pharmacist prescription for this patient, and the pharmacist may prescribe if every operative condition is met. The error the scenario invites is to apply a statutory direction to rulemakers as if it were an adopted rule and to supply a time frame that neither the regulation nor the Department's letter states.

worked_examples.scenario: Before prescribing for the first time, a pharmacist completes an employer course that is not accredited by ACPE or IPCE. It covers the mechanism of action and types of hormonal contraceptives, patient eligibility, patient education on use, risks and benefits, and documenting patient care visits, but nothing on reducing the risk of sexually transmitted infections, and she keeps no record of completing it. She plans to send the prescriptions she issues to her employer's other store nearest each patient's home for dispensing.
steps: Accreditation: Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 recommends ACPE or IPCE accredited programs but does not require accreditation, so the course's lack of accreditation is not by itself the defect.

Objectives: the letter says the program objectives must include educating patients on strategies to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections, so a course without that objective does not meet the letter.
Approval and timing: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b)1 requires a training program approved by the board of registration in pharmacy, completed prior to prescribing.
Documentation: the letter requires documentation of completed training to be provided upon request, and keeping no record leaves her unable to provide it.

Registration: the letter states that no Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration is required as long as the prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location, and dispensing at another store takes her outside that statement.
worked_examples.resolution: She should not prescribe until she has completed training that addresses all five objectives and meets the regulation's approval requirement, with documentation she can provide, and she should dispense at the location where she prescribes or ask the Drug Control Program before doing otherwise. The error the scenario invites is to fix on accreditation, which is only recommended, while missing the required objective, the documentation and the single-location condition.

worked_examples.scenario: A person hands a pharmacy a written prescription for doxycycline that bears 'E.P.T.' where the patient's name and address would go; the prescriber's note says it is for the partner of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia. A technician starts to add it to the index patient's profile. The pharmacist on duty is unwilling to fill it and tells the person to take it back to the prescriber.
steps: Form: 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) calls for a separate prescription for the sex partner bearing the partner's name or 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' where the patient's name and address are noted, and this prescription bears 'E.P.T.' for the partner of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia.

Format rules: 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) excepts such a prescription from the electronic prescription requirement, so a written prescription is permitted, and 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) allows its name and address to be left blank.

Profile and label: Policy 2020-08, as the dispensing procedure under that authority, directs the pharmacy to create a patient profile and prescription label using the designation in place of the patient's name and address, so the index patient's profile is not where it belongs.
The unwilling pharmacist: under Policy 2020-08 a pharmacist who is unable or unwilling to fill an expedited partner therapy prescription must refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy.
worked_examples.resolution: If the pharmacy fills it, the profile and label use a designation in place of the name and address, not the index patient's record; if the pharmacist will not fill it, the pharmacist must refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy. The error the scenario invites is to treat sending the person back to the prescriber as enough, when the policy's instruction is referral to an alternate pharmacy.

worked_examples.scenario: On the same afternoon a pharmacy receives two partner prescriptions without names. The first bears 'EPT' and is for the partner of a patient diagnosed with gonorrhea only, and the prescriber points out that M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B now refers to other sexually transmitted infections. The second is for the partner of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia, its patient name and address field is entirely empty, and the prescriber points to 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).
steps: First prescription: s. 121B authorizes regulations for Chlamydia trachomatis and other sexually transmitted infections suitable for expedited partner treatment as further defined in regulation by the department, and 105 CMR 700.003(H) provides expedited partner therapy for the treatment of chlamydia infection.
Policy 2020-08 states that it applies only to the treatment of chlamydia infection, so its dispensing procedures do not reach a partner prescription for gonorrhea only.

Second prescription: 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) does allow the name and address to be left blank on a prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7), the exception for expedited partner therapy prescriptions for chlamydia intended for dispensing to the patient's partner.
But 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) and Policy 2020-08 describe the partner prescription as bearing the partner's name or one of the three designations in that place, and the second prescription bears neither.
worked_examples.resolution: Neither prescription fits expedited partner therapy as the regulation and the policy describe it: the first falls outside their chlamydia provision, and the second lacks the name or designation those texts call for, so the safe course with each is to contact the prescriber before filling. The error the scenario invites is to treat the broader statutory words, or the format regulation's blank-field allowance, as settling the question on its own.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(a)(i), who may prescribe and dispense, what, and to whom?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A registered pharmacist; hormonal contraceptive patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives; to any person, regardless of whether the person has evidence of a previous prescription from a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which session law inserted s. 19F in chapter 94C, and as of what date did that act take effect?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Section 42 of chapter 28 of the Acts of 2023. Except as otherwise specified, the act took effect as of July 1, 2023, and no other date is specified for section 42.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What did section 39 of chapter 14 of the Acts of 2025 do to s. 19F?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It struck out and replaced subsection (a): the contraceptive authority now sits in clause (i), and a new clause (ii) addresses medications for HIV and sexually transmitted infections, a subject not taught here. The act was an emergency law approved on August 5, 2025.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: With whom must the department consult under s. 19F(b), and whose guidelines must it consider?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The board of registration in medicine, the board of registration in pharmacy and the division of medical assistance; guidelines established by the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: s. 19F itself bars a pharmacist from prescribing for a returning patient who has no evidence of a clinical visit.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. Section 19F(c)(ii)(B) directs the rules adopted under s. 19F(b) to impose that bar within a time frame those rules are to set. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) states no time frame and no such prohibition, and Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 says lack of a clinical visit does not preclude a prescription with refills.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Name the five requirements 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b) places on a registered pharmacist prescribing these products.
retrieval_prompts.answer: Complete a training program approved by the board of registration in pharmacy prior to prescribing; provide a self-screening risk assessment tool the patient uses prior to prescribing; refer the patient to a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner, if applicable, or advise the patient to consult one; provide a written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; and dispense as soon as practicable after issuing the prescription.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under which heading does 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) sit, and on what terms does it grant the authority?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Exemptions from Requirement to Register, in 105 CMR 700.004(B). It grants the authority to prescribe and dispense to any person in accordance with guidance issued by the department.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What is the most supply a pharmacist-generated contraceptive prescription may be for under the Department's letter?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Up to, but not more than, a 12-month supply.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Is there a minimum patient age, and does an over-the-counter product fall outside pharmacist prescribing?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No minimum age: the letter permits prescribing to patients of any age. Over-the-counter status is no bar: the letter applies regardless of whether the product is over-the-counter or prescription-only.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What five objectives must the contraceptive prescribing training include, and is ACPE or IPCE accreditation required?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Describing the mechanism of action and differentiating types of hormonal contraceptive products; assessing patient eligibility and recommended products; educating patients on proper use, risks and benefits; educating patients on strategies to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections; and documenting patient care visits. Accreditation is recommended, not required, and documentation of completed training must be provided upon request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: On what condition does the Department's letter say a pharmacist needs no Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration to prescribe these products?
retrieval_prompts.answer: As long as the prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What identifier must the prescribing pharmacist obtain, and is enrollment in MassHealth required?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A National Provider Identifier (NPI). MassHealth enrollment for the limited purpose of ordering and referring is encouraged, not required.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What alternative to referral or advice does the Department's letter name, and what course satisfies both the letter and the regulation?
retrieval_prompts.answer: With the patient's consent, notifying the patient's primary care practitioner. Referring the patient, if applicable, or advising the patient to consult a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner in every case, and also notifying the primary care practitioner where the patient consents, satisfies both.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under 105 CMR 700.003(H), who may provide expedited partner therapy, and for which infection?
retrieval_prompts.answer: A registered physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or nurse midwife, for the treatment of chlamydia infection in the sex partner or partners of a patient diagnosed with it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a separate partner prescription carry where the patient's name and address would be noted?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Either the name of the sex partner or the words 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' (105 CMR 700.003(H)(3); Policy 2020-08, citing 105 CMR 700.003(H), describes the same two ways).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Must an expedited partner therapy prescription for chlamydia be electronic, and may its name and address be left blank?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It need not be electronic: 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) excepts it, so it may be written or oral. Under 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) the name and address may be left blank, but 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) and the Board's policy still call for the partner's name or a designation in that place.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under Policy 2020-08, how does the pharmacy profile and label an expedited partner therapy prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It creates a patient profile and prescription label using 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the patient's name and address, as a dispensing procedure under the authority in M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B and 105 CMR 700.003(H).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must a pharmacist who is unable or unwilling to fill an expedited partner therapy prescription do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy, under Policy 2020-08.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Does Policy 2020-08 reach a partner prescription for gonorrhea because s. 121B now mentions other sexually transmitted infections?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. The policy states that it applies only to the treatment of chlamydia infection, and 105 CMR 700.003(H) provides expedited partner therapy for chlamydia; s. 121B reaches other infections as further defined in regulation.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who counsels the patient about expedited partner therapy and provides the information sheet for the partner?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or nurse midwife, who provides a Department information sheet, or a comparable one, whenever possible (105 CMR 700.003(H)(4)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Under Board Policy 2023-05, what happens when a family planning medication is not immediately available for dispensing on a valid prescription, and what does the policy say about refusing to fill?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The licensed pharmacy and/or licensed pharmacist ensures the patient's access in a timely manner by refilling stock, contacting the prescriber for a reasonable alternative medication, transferring the prescription to another pharmacy where the medication is readily available, or another manner such as mail order or central fill. Refusing to stock, dispense or fill a valid prescription or order for family planning medications, or impeding access, will be in violation of 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) and practice standards.

quick_review.text: A registered pharmacist may prescribe and dispense hormonal contraceptive patches and self-administered oral hormonal contraceptives to any person, regardless of whether the person has evidence of a previous prescription (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F(a)(i)).

Section 19F(b) and (c) state what the Department's rules shall establish, require and prohibit; a requirement binds the pharmacist through 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15), which grants the authority in accordance with Department guidance.

105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b): Board-approved training prior to prescribing; a self-screening tool the patient uses prior to prescribing; referral, if applicable, or advice to consult; a written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; dispensing as soon as practicable after issuing the prescription.
105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(c): a pharmacist shall not require a patient to schedule an appointment for the prescribing or dispensing.
No clinical-visit time frame or prohibition appears in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15), and Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125 says lack of a clinical visit does not preclude a prescription with refills.

DCP 26-08-125: FDA-approved products only, over-the-counter or prescription-only, patients of any age, no more than a 12-month supply, prescribed only in accordance with the manufacturer's approved labeling or statewide guidance.

DCP 26-08-125: the pharmacist obtains an NPI and maintains continued competency; counseling and education on proper use, risks and side effects are conducted; all activities related to the prescribing and dispensing are documented and readily available.
Training addresses five objectives, including strategies to reduce the risk of sexually transmitted infections; ACPE or IPCE accreditation is recommended; documentation is provided upon request.

No Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration is required as long as the prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location, and there is no requirement to prescribe these medications.

Expedited partner therapy under 105 CMR 700.003(H): a registered physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or nurse midwife; chlamydia infection; an appropriate therapeutic agent in Schedule VI for immediate treatment.

M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B reaches Chlamydia trachomatis and other sexually transmitted infections suitable for expedited partner treatment as further defined in regulation; the regulation provides for chlamydia.
The separate partner prescription bears the partner's name or 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' where the patient's name and address are noted.
105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) excepts expedited partner therapy prescriptions for chlamydia from the electronic prescription requirement, and 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) lets their name and address be left blank.

Policy 2020-08, the dispensing procedures under that authority, applies only to the treatment of chlamydia infection; the pharmacy profiles and labels using a designation in place of the patient's name and address.
A pharmacist unable or unwilling to fill an expedited partner therapy prescription must refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy.

Policy 2023-05, applying 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f): pharmacies licensed by the Board maintain a continuous, sufficient supply of family planning medications, including emergency contraception and contraceptive prescriptions, and refusing to stock, dispense or fill a valid prescription or order for them, or impeding access, will be in violation of 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) and practice standards.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks a pharmacist to prescribe a contraceptive.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the product is an FDA-approved hormonal contraceptive patch or self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive; whether it is over-the-counter or prescription-only does not matter. Any other product is outside s. 19F(a)(i) and the Department's letter.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist has not completed contraceptive prescribing training.
decision_logic.action: Do not prescribe. Complete a program approved by the board of registration in pharmacy that addresses the five objectives in Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125, and keep documentation that can be provided upon request.

decision_logic.condition: The patient arrives without an appointment.
decision_logic.action: Do not require one: 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(c) provides that a pharmacist shall not require a patient to schedule an appointment for the prescribing or dispensing.

decision_logic.condition: The patient is a minor, or has never had a contraceptive prescription.
decision_logic.action: Neither is a bar: the letter permits prescribing to patients of any age, and the statute and regulation allow prescribing regardless of evidence of a previous prescription.

Have the patient complete the pharmacy-provided self-screening risk assessment tool based on the current United States Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, and prescribe only in accordance with the manufacturer's approved labeling or statewide guidance.

decision_logic.condition: The patient previously received a pharmacist prescription and has had no clinical visit since.
decision_logic.action: Do not treat that as a bar. 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) contains no time frame or prohibition, and the letter says lack of a clinical visit does not preclude a prescription with refills; apply the conditions that do operate.
Generate a valid prescription for no more than a 12-month supply, keeping refills within that ceiling as the safe course, with the pharmacist's NPI obtained.

Dispense as soon as practicable; provide the written record of the product prescribed and dispensed; refer the patient, if applicable, or advise the patient to consult a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner, and notify the primary care practitioner as well with the patient's consent. Under the letter, counseling and education on proper use, risks and side effects are conducted, and all activities related to the prescribing and dispensing are documented and readily available.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist's prescription would be dispensed at a different pharmacy location.
decision_logic.action: The letter's no-registration statement covers prescribing and dispensing at a single pharmacy location; dispense where the pharmacist prescribes, or ask the Drug Control Program first.

decision_logic.condition: A valid contraceptive prescription written by another prescriber cannot be filled at once because the product is not immediately available.
decision_logic.action: Under Policy 2023-05, ensure the patient's access in a timely manner: refill the stock, contact the prescriber for a reasonable alternative medication, transfer the prescription to another pharmacy where the medication is readily available, or use another manner such as mail order or central fill.

decision_logic.condition: A pharmacy receives a prescription for the unexamined sex partner of a patient.
decision_logic.action: Ask whether it fits 105 CMR 700.003(H): a patient diagnosed with chlamydia infection, and a prescriber who is a physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or nurse midwife. A partner prescription for another infection is outside 105 CMR 700.003(H) and the dispensing procedures of Policy 2020-08.

decision_logic.condition: The partner prescription is checked for form.
decision_logic.action: Look for a separate prescription bearing the partner's name or 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' where the patient's name and address are noted. It may be written or oral and its name and address may be left blank; if the field bears neither a name nor a designation, contact the prescriber.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy fills an expedited partner therapy prescription bearing a designation.
decision_logic.action: Create the patient profile and prescription label using 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the patient's name and address.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacist is unable or unwilling to fill an expedited partner therapy prescription.
decision_logic.action: Refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy.

ma_vs_federal.text: The prescribing authority is Massachusetts law: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 19F and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15). Federal law enters through the Department's letter, which confines the pharmacist to FDA-approved medications, requires prescribing only in accordance with the manufacturer's approved labeling or statewide guidance, and treats a product's over-the-counter or prescription-only status as no bar.

The self-screening tool is to be based on the current United States Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, but the obligation to provide and use such a tool comes from 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) and the Department's letter.

105 CMR 700.003(H)(1) requires expedited partner therapy to accord with the applicable guidelines of the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, and M.G.L. c. 111, s. 121B names the Center for Disease Control's Sexually Transmitted Infections Treatment Guidelines among the national standards; those federal guidelines apply here because Massachusetts law points to them.

exceptions.text: No previous practitioner prescription is needed: s. 19F(a)(i) and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(a) allow prescribing regardless of evidence of one, provided the requirements of 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b) and (c) are met.
Referral is qualified: the pharmacist refers the patient to a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner if applicable, or instead advises the patient to consult one.
Registration: the Department's letter states that no Massachusetts Controlled Substance Registration is required as long as the prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location.
Refills: lack of a clinical visit with a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner does not preclude a pharmacist from issuing a prescription with refills.
A practitioner may dispense the expedited partner therapy agent directly instead of prescribing it, in a separate, properly labeled container for the sex partner.
Expedited partner therapy prescriptions for chlamydia intended for dispensing to the patient's partner need not be electronic and may be written or oral (105 CMR 721.070(A)(7)).

The patient's name and address may be left blank on a prescription issued under 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) (105 CMR 721.020(D)(4)), with the partner's name or a designation standing in that place under 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3).
The partner information sheet is qualified: the practitioner provides the Department sheet, or a comparable one, whenever possible.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: As of July 1, 2023 (St. 2023, c. 28, ss. 42 and 115)
timing_deadlines.consequence: Section 19F, including its direction to the Department to adopt rules, is part of chapter 94C from that date.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: St. 2025, c. 14, s. 39, in an emergency law approved August 5, 2025
timing_deadlines.consequence: Subsection (a) holds the contraceptive authority in clause (i) and a separate HIV and sexually transmitted infection authority in clause (ii).
A pharmacist who has not completed a Board-approved program addressing the letter's five objectives does not prescribe.
The patient uses the pharmacy-provided tool first, and prescribing follows.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: As soon as practicable after the pharmacist issues the prescription
timing_deadlines.consequence: A pharmacist who issues the prescription and then defers supplying an available product to a later visit does not meet the requirement.
The patient is referred, if applicable, or advised to consult a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner at that point.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Up to, but not more than, 12 months
timing_deadlines.consequence: A prescription for a longer supply exceeds the Department's ceiling.

timing_deadlines.event: Clinical visit after a previous pharmacist prescription
timing_deadlines.timeframe: To be set by rules under s. 19F(b)(ii); no time frame appears in 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) or Circular Letter DCP 26-08-125
timing_deadlines.consequence: No operative clinical-visit bar applies, and the letter says lack of a clinical visit does not preclude a prescription with refills.
Documentation of completed training must be provided when it is requested.
The letter rescinds and replaces DCP 25-04-124.

timing_deadlines.event: Section 121B amended to refer to other sexually transmitted infections
timing_deadlines.consequence: The statute reaches other infections as further defined in regulation, while 105 CMR 700.003(H) provides expedited partner therapy for chlamydia.

forms_records.text: Self-screening risk assessment tool: provided by the pharmacy, based on the current United States Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use, and used by the patient before the pharmacist prescribes.
Prescription: the prescribing pharmacist generates a valid prescription for up to, but not more than, a 12-month supply.
Written record: provided to the patient, of the hormonal contraceptive patch or self-administered oral hormonal contraceptive prescribed and dispensed.
Pharmacy documentation: all activities related to the prescribing and dispensing are documented and readily available.
Training documentation: documentation of completed training must be provided upon request.
National Provider Identifier: the prescribing pharmacist must obtain one.
Separate partner prescription: bears the partner's name or 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' where the patient's name and address are noted.
Form of the partner prescription: it may be written or oral under the exception in 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7), and its name and address may be left blank under 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).

Pharmacy patient profile and prescription label for expedited partner therapy: created, under the dispensing procedures of Policy 2020-08, using 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the patient's name and address.
Practitioner-dispensed expedited partner therapy: the therapeutic agent is provided in a separate, properly labeled container for the sex partner.

Partner information sheet: a Department sheet or a comparable one, provided by the practitioner whenever possible, with pertinent information about procedures for taking the medication, avoiding sexual activity as required during treatment, possible allergic reactions and avoiding future infection.

role_duties.duty: Shall adopt rules, in consultation with the board of registration in medicine, the board of registration in pharmacy and the division of medical assistance and in consideration of ACOG guidelines, establishing standard procedures for pharmacist prescribing and the clinical-visit time frame, and containing the requirements and prohibitions listed in s. 19F(c).

role_duties.role: Board of Registration in Pharmacy (contraceptive prescribing)
role_duties.duty: Its approval is what the training program must carry: s. 19F(c)(i)(A) and 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b)1 refer to a training program approved by the board of registration in pharmacy, completed before the pharmacist prescribes.

Completes Board-approved training addressing the letter's five objectives before prescribing; provides the self-screening tool; prescribes only FDA-approved patches or oral hormonal contraceptives in accordance with the labeling or statewide guidance, for no more than a 12-month supply; obtains an NPI; does not require an appointment.

Dispenses as soon as practicable after issuing the prescription; provides the written record; refers the patient, if applicable, or advises consultation with a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner, notifying the primary care practitioner with consent as the letter allows. The letter's conditions that counseling and education on proper use, risks and side effects be conducted, and that all activities related to the prescribing and dispensing be documented and readily available, apply to the prescribing.
Is under no requirement to prescribe these medications, and a pharmacist who prescribes maintains continued competency regarding current guidelines.
Uses the pharmacy-provided self-screening risk assessment tool before the pharmacist prescribes.

role_duties.role: Pharmacy located in Massachusetts and licensed by the Board (family planning medications)
role_duties.duty: Maintains a continuous, sufficient supply of family planning medications, including emergency contraception and contraceptive prescriptions, which Policy 2023-05 treats as necessary to meet the usual needs of the community under 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f).

role_duties.role: Licensed pharmacy and/or licensed pharmacist (family planning medication not immediately available)
role_duties.duty: Ensures the patient's access in a timely manner by one of the routes Policy 2023-05 lists; the policy states that refusing to stock, dispense or fill a valid prescription or order for family planning medications, or impeding access, will be in violation of 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) and practice standards.

role_duties.role: Department of Public Health (expedited partner therapy)
role_duties.duty: Shall promulgate regulations, in consultation with the board of registration in medicine, authorizing expedited partner treatment by the named practitioners for Chlamydia trachomatis and other sexually transmitted infections as further defined in regulation.

role_duties.role: Physician, physician assistant, certified nurse practitioner or nurse midwife providing expedited partner therapy
role_duties.duty: May prescribe or dispense an appropriate Schedule VI agent for the sex partner of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia infection; issues a separate partner prescription bearing the partner's name or a designation, or dispenses in a separate, properly labeled container; counsels the patient and, whenever possible, provides the information sheet.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist receiving an expedited partner therapy prescription for chlamydia
role_duties.duty: May receive it as a written or oral prescription, because 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) does not require it to be electronic. The place for the patient's name and address carries the partner's name or 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' as 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3) describes, although the name and address themselves may be left blank under 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4).

role_duties.role: Pharmacy filling an expedited partner therapy prescription
role_duties.duty: Creates the patient profile and prescription label using 'Expedited Partner Therapy,' 'E.P.T.' or 'EPT' in place of the patient's name and address, under the dispensing procedures of Policy 2020-08.

role_duties.role: Pharmacist unable or unwilling to fill an expedited partner therapy prescription
role_duties.duty: Must refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy.

common_traps.text: Requiring an appointment for contraceptive prescribing or dispensing, however reasonable the workflow reason; 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(c) says a pharmacist shall not.

Applying s. 19F(c)(ii)(B) as if it bound pharmacists today. It is a direction to the Department's rules; 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15) has no clinical-visit time frame or prohibition, and the letter says lack of a clinical visit does not preclude a prescription with refills.
Inventing an age limit; the Department's letter permits prescribing to patients of any age.
Requiring a prior prescription from a primary care or reproductive health care practitioner; the statute and regulation allow prescribing regardless of evidence of one.
Treating ACPE or IPCE accreditation as mandatory while overlooking the five required objectives and the documentation to be provided upon request.
Reading the letter's registration statement as unconditional; it applies as long as the prescribing and dispensing both occur at a single pharmacy location.

Prescribing a product outside the two statutory types or one that is not FDA-approved; the letter confines pharmacist prescribing to FDA-approved medications authorized by s. 19F and contained in the letter.
Issuing a prescription for more than a 12-month supply.
Issuing the prescription and then telling the patient to come back later for a product that is available; dispensing must follow as soon as practicable.

Reading the letter's notification alternative as displacing the regulation; 105 CMR 700.004(B)(15)(b)3 still calls for referral, if applicable, or advice to consult, so the safe course is to refer or advise and also to notify with consent.
Assuming a pharmacist must prescribe on request; the letter states that there is no requirement to prescribe these medications.

Declining a valid contraceptive prescription written by another prescriber on the strength of the letter's statement that there is no requirement to prescribe, or of the expedited partner therapy referral route; Policy 2023-05 states that refusing to stock, dispense or fill a valid prescription or order for family planning medications, or impeding access, violates 247 CMR 9.19(1)(f) and practice standards.

Treating a partner prescription for gonorrhea as expedited partner therapy under Policy 2020-08 because s. 121B now mentions other sexually transmitted infections; the policy applies only to chlamydia and the regulation provides for chlamydia.
Counting a pharmacist among the practitioners who may provide expedited partner therapy under 105 CMR 700.003(H).
Putting the partner's prescription on the index patient's profile; the policy directs a profile and label using a designation in place of the patient's name and address.
Sending the person back to the prescriber when unwilling to fill; the policy requires the pharmacist to refer the patient to an alternate pharmacy.

Treating an entirely empty patient field as acceptable because 105 CMR 721.020(D)(4) lets the name and address be left blank; the partner's name or a designation still belongs there under 105 CMR 700.003(H)(3).
Assuming an expedited partner therapy prescription for chlamydia must be electronic; 105 CMR 721.070(A)(7) lets it be written or oral.

drug_examples.teaching_point: Neither 105 CMR 700.003(H) nor Policy 2020-08 names a drug; the regulation speaks of an appropriate therapeutic agent in Schedule VI for the partner of a patient diagnosed with chlamydia infection. Whether a doxycycline prescription for an unexamined partner is expedited partner therapy turns on that diagnosis and on the separate partner prescription, and naming doxycycline does not bring a partner prescription for another infection within the regulation or the policy.
